nodes.text: Continued progress on ultra-low-power, on-device machine learning (TinyML) has been limited by the lack of a widely accepted, reproducible benchmark for comparing systems built for it.

On-device inference under a milliwatt enables always-on, battery-powered, privacy-preserving applications and avoids the higher energy cost of wireless transmission, but only if systems built for it can be fairly compared.

The closest prior benchmarks: CoreMark profiles simple algorithms but not ML workloads; MLMark profiles real ML workloads but needs GB-scale memory and has no power measurement; MLPerf's inference suite excludes MCU-class hardware outright.

None of these characterizes the accuracy-latency-energy tradeoffs of real inference on microcontroller-class, milliwatt-power hardware; the authors state directly that a benchmark treating power as first-class and fitting TinyML's constraints is needed.

Can one benchmark suite fit the memory/power constraints of microcontroller-class devices, measure accuracy, latency, and energy together, and let a fair comparison be made across the field's heterogeneous hardware and software?
TinyML hardware (microcontrollers, DSPs, small NN accelerators) typically runs at 10-250 MHz and under 50 mW, several orders of magnitude tighter than smartphone-class ML deployment.
nodes.audience_note: Adjacent ML researchers know 'edge inference' at phone/GPU scale but not the microcontroller-class resource envelope; this anchor is given before any benchmark-design detail.

nodes.text: Build and validate a benchmark suite that pairs four fixed reference tasks with a standardized latency/accuracy/energy measurement harness and a modular open/closed submission structure.

Four reference benchmarks -- keyword spotting, visual wake words, image classification, anomaly detection -- each with its own dataset, model, and quality threshold chosen for MCU-class deployment; a shared closed/open division scheme; a shared measurement protocol.
Design each benchmark's task, dataset, model, and accuracy/AUC threshold from the constraints and prior practice specific to that use case.
The visual-wake-words reference model reaches about 86% accuracy on the preprocessed MSCOCO2014 test set; the closed-division threshold is set to 80%.
The image-classification reference model reaches 86.5% accuracy on a 200-image CIFAR-10 test subset; the threshold is set to 85%.
The keyword-spotting reference model reaches 92.2% accuracy (91.6%/91.7% for the quantized reference model); the threshold is set to 90%.
The anomaly-detection reference autoencoder reaches AUC 0.88 (fp32) / 0.86 (quantized); the threshold is set to 0.85.
Run the full measurement harness on the reference board across all four benchmarks, then open the suite to external submitters for a first round.

All four reference implementations, run on the NUCLEO-L4R5ZI board, meet their accuracy targets, with latency and energy spanning a wide range across the four tasks (qualitative summary; exact per-benchmark figures are not recoverable from the extracted text).

The first submission round (June 2021) produced five results: four closed-division (ARM MCU; RISC-V MCU; Raspberry Pi 4 via a hardware-agnostic toolchain; a neural-network accelerator) and one open-division (an FPGA via a high-level-synthesis flow), each demonstrating a different part of the stack.

Across the round: 8-bit integer was the dominant numerical format, frameworks ranged from an open interpreter to hardware-specific compilers, measured power spanned microwatts to watts, and no submitter changed the training dataset.

The suite's modular, three-metric design was flexible enough to let very different hardware/software stacks report comparable results, while first-round practice stayed concentrated on models, frameworks, and hardware rather than data.

An open, modular, three-metric (accuracy/latency/energy) benchmark suite for ultra-low-power ML, with four reference implementations that meet their targets on a common board and a first external submission round that exercised the suite across five different hardware/software stacks.

The suite's own account of streaming/pre-processing measurement is unresolved, and the closed division supports only FC/CNN architectures, with long-term multi-version stability a stated goal rather than a demonstrated property.
The authors themselves flag a dual-use and e-waste caveat on the suite's broader benefit.

The evidence for adoption and flexibility comes from one submission round of five results on one reference board, without published per-submission numeric scores or run-to-run variance in the paper text itself.
A modular, three-metric benchmark can let heterogeneous TinyML hardware and software stacks report comparable results without forcing every submitter onto the same stack.

Future rounds are expected to add benchmarks/architectures (e.g., RNNs) and application domains (wearables, medical, environmental monitoring), and to show whether dataset-centric submissions and long-term stability follow.

experiment_chains.hypothesis: Each of the four benchmark tasks can be specified (dataset + model + threshold) and measured (latency/accuracy/energy) within the constraints of one microcontroller-class reference board.
experiment_chains.falsifier: A reference implementation fails to meet its own accuracy threshold, or cannot be run and measured on the reference board under the defined protocol.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: Fixing one reference implementation per benchmark, run through a single shared measurement harness on one reference board, checks whether the suite's task and metric definitions are achievable at all before asking whether third parties can reproduce or improve on them.
experiment_chains.next: If the reference implementations run and meet target on one board, the next question is whether independent submitters, on different hardware and software, can use the same suite and produce comparable, informative results -- the v0.5 submission round.

experiment_chains.hypothesis: The suite's modular closed/open division and shared three-metric protocol let independent organizations, on heterogeneous hardware and software, submit results that are comparable and that each highlight a different stack-level contribution.
experiment_chains.falsifier: Submitters are unable to use the suite on hardware other than the reference board, submissions cluster on a single stack layer, or the closed/open distinction fails to separate comparable from non-comparable results.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: An open call for submissions, checked by the submitter group and a review committee against the published run rules, tests the suite under real third-party conditions that a single reference implementation cannot.
experiment_chains.next: Last experiment reported in this paper; the Discussion interprets what the round's diversity, and its one clear gap (no dataset-level submissions), mean for the suite's design and for TinyML practice.
